content: These references include research on directly observed therapy (DOT), community-based interventions, adherence strategies, and innovative approaches to improve TB treatment outcomes. 1. In Ensenada, Mexico, it was observed that not all DOTS (Directly Observed Treatment, Short-course) programs are equally effective in managing tuberculosis. (Int J Tuberc Lung Dis. 2007;11(3):289–92.) 2. A study in Thailand demonstrated that directly observed therapy significantly improved tuberculosis treatment outcomes. (PLoS One. 2008;3(8):e3089.) 3. Research in Thailand found that directly observed treatment reduced default rates among foreign tuberculosis patients. (Int J Tuberc Lung Dis. 2009;13(2):232–7.) 4. In Carapicuíba, Brazil, the implementation of the directly observed treatment short-course (DOTS) strategy improved compliance with tuberculosis treatment. (J Bras Pneumol. 2011;37(2):223–31.) 5. A study in Kenya compared rural and urban settings and found that community health workers positively influenced tuberculosis treatment adherence. (PLoS One. 2014;9(2):e88937.) 6. In India, both directly observed and self-administered tuberculosis treatments were evaluated in a chronic, low-intensity conflict setting, showing varying levels of effectiveness. (PLoS One. 2014;9(3):e92131.) 7. Supervised intermittent therapy was found to be effective for tuberculosis treatment in HIV-infected patients in a study conducted in the United States. (AIDS. 1994;8(8):1103–8.) 8. A study in Russia demonstrated that food incentives improved adherence to tuberculosis drug treatment among homeless patients. (Scand J Caring Sci. 2013;27(1):117–22.) 9. In Spain, directly observed treatment in pharmacies was compared to self-administered therapy, showing better outcomes with the former. (Int J Tuberc Lung Dis. 2006;10(2):215–21.) 10. Research in South Africa highlighted the contribution of traditional healers to rural tuberculosis control programs. (Int J Tuberc Lung Dis. 2003;7(9):S86–91.) 11. In Ethiopia, innovative community-based approaches doubled tuberculosis case notification rates and improved treatment outcomes. (PLoS One. 2013;8(5):e63174.) 12. A study in Thailand evaluated the effectiveness of a health education program aimed at improving tuberculosis treatment compliance among migrants. (J Med Assoc Thai. 2013;96(3):365–73.) 13. In New York City, video directly observed therapy was shown to enhance tuberculosis treatment management. (Int J Tuberc Lung Dis. 2016;20(5):588–93.) 14. A randomized controlled trial in Timor-Leste demonstrated that food incentives improved tuberculosis treatment completion rates. (BMJ. 2009;339:b4248.) 15. In South Africa, economic support was found to improve tuberculosis treatment outcomes in a pragmatic cluster-randomized controlled trial. (Trials. 2013;14(1):154.) 16. A study in India revealed that mobile-phone medication reminders significantly improved adherence to tuberculosis treatment. (Southeast Asian J Trop Med Public Health. 2011;42(6):1444–51.) 17. In Pakistan, a cohort analysis showed the effectiveness of directly observed treatment outcomes for tuberculosis patients in urban settings. (Int J Tuberc Lung Dis. 2011;15(1):90–6.) 18. Research in South Africa demonstrated that community tracer teams positively impacted tuberculosis treatment outcomes. (BMC Public Health. 2012;12(1):621.) 19. In Ethiopia, health extension workers were shown to improve tuberculosis case detection and treatment success in a community-randomized trial. (PLoS One. 2009;4(5):e5443.) 20. A study in India found that psychotherapy improved compliance with tuberculosis treatment. (Respiration. 2005;72(4):375–80.) 21. In Tanzania, a randomized controlled trial compared community-based and institutional-based directly observed short-course treatment for tuberculosis, finding community-based approaches to be effective. (Trop Med Int Health. 2003;8(3):204–10.) 22. In Haiti, managing medication compliance for tuberculosis patients using medication monitors was found to be effective. (Int J Tuberc Lung Dis. 2002;6(4):313–9.) 23. A study in Malawi evaluated a knowledge translation intervention to improve tuberculosis care and outcomes, showing promising results. (Implement Sci. 2015;10(1):38.) 24. In Brazil, a community intervention beyond DOTS in a socially vulnerable area improved tuberculosis control. (Int J Tuberc Lung Dis. 2013;17(12):1581–6.) 25. In India, a randomized study compared two policies for managing default in outpatients collecting tuberculosis drugs, highlighting the importance of patient follow-up. (Tubercle. 1981;62(2):103–12.) 26. In Thailand, a study demonstrated that automated telephone reminders improved tuberculosis care. (Med Care. 1994;32(4):380–9.) 27. In Nepal, family-member DOTS and community DOTS were compared in a cluster-randomized controlled trial, showing the effectiveness of community-based approaches. (Lancet. 2006;367(9514):903–9.) 28. In Tanzania, a randomized controlled trial evaluated the effectiveness of community-based directly observed treatment for tuberculosis in an urban setting, showing positive outcomes. (Int J Tuberc Lung Dis. 2004;8(10):1248–54.) 29. In South Africa, lay health worker-supported tuberculosis treatment adherence was studied using an interrupted time-series design, demonstrating its efficacy. (Int J Tuberc Lung Dis. 2011;15(1):84–9.) 30. In India, a randomized controlled trial evaluated the impact of nutritional supplements on patients with newly diagnosed tuberculosis and wasting, showing improved outcomes. (Singapore Med J. 2010;51(12):957.) 31. In Ethiopia, community-based tuberculosis care through TB clubs in rural areas was found to be effective. (Soc Sci Med. 2003;56(10):2009–18.) 32. In Zambia, integrating tuberculosis treatment into a community-based home care program for persons living with HIV/AIDS improved treatment outcomes. (Int J Tuberc Lung Dis. 2003;7(9):S92–8.) 33. In Botswana, home-based care was found to be more cost-effective than hospital care for chronically ill tuberculosis patients. (Int J Tuberc Lung Dis. 2003;7(9):S80–5.) 34. In Iraq, community participation improved treatment outcomes and compliance among DOTS patients. (East Mediterr Health J. 2003;9(4):709–17.) 35. In New Delhi, India, community-mediated domiciliary DOTS execution was studied, showing its feasibility and effectiveness. (Indian J Tuberc. 2003;50:143–50.) 36. In South India, a randomized study evaluated the effectiveness of two policies for managing default in outpatients collecting tuberculosis drugs, emphasizing the importance of patient follow-up.
